properties.chose:
SETTLED 2026-09-28 on Anthony's word, after issue #616 and the measured forgery (fact:root-cause-an-exposed-server-accepts-any-callers-signature-because-the-boundary-where-write-rules-attach-was-named-and-no-rule-was-chosen-2026-09-28). His words: "Go with the solution that is most right. I don't like quick or patch efforts that don't fix at root. Reflow2 is evolving to being used in something like flo2.io, but at work, I still use it locally (how we have been using prior to flo2.io)."

CHOSEN: option (e), with a rule for EVERY deliberate exposure, so the boundary this decision drew in August finally has rules on its far side.
· LOCAL IS UNCHANGED: stdio, --shared, and --http on loopback. The caller's identity is trusted as today, and there is no sign-in. This is the way Anthony works, and req:reflow2-keeps-working-entirely-on-one-machine holds.
· AN EXPOSED SERVER (one given --http-allow-host) DECLARES HOW IDENTITY IS ESTABLISHED, and reflow2 enforces it:
  - OIDC (option e): reflow2 is an OAuth 2.0 resource server. It validates the Bearer JWT (the signature against the issuer's published keys, plus iss, aud and exp) and may require a claim. It serves /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource and answers 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header naming it, so MCP clients discover the sign-in and run it themselves. The person is the contributor an operator-configured mapping derives from a verified claim. Every AUTHORED_BY a call writes (author or approver) is for that contributor, and a call naming anyone else is refused. reflow2 verifies; it never issues identity (no sign-in flow, no sessions, no user table).
  - A TRUSTED GATEWAY: the operator declares that a gateway in front authenticates and names the person on each call (flo2's case). reflow2 trusts writes_for and approver as given, and says so in the handshake.
  - UNDECLARED: the server still serves reads and proposals, and REFUSES every settling write (an approver, or a status past proposed), naming the flags that would allow it. Option (d) becomes the fallback, so exposure never again silently trusts anyone.

WHY THE OTHERS LOST: (a) alone trusts a header reflow2 cannot check was stripped. (d) alone leaves a team with no single machine unable to approve anything. (b) and (c) do not establish who the person is.

WHAT THIS NARROWS: reason 1 of dec:the-registry-root-is-the-tenant-boundary ("reflow2 has no authentication and is not getting any") and the architecture Anthony settled in flo2's design on 2026-09-20 ("reflow2 stays an engine and grows no authentication"). reflow2 now verifies a token when an operator turns it on, and still never issues identity. flo2 stays its own resource server and declares the trusted-gateway mode.
properties.decision:
Anthony, 2026-08-26: *"can't we do authentication at another layer (like middleware) so that reflow2 doesn't have to worry about authentication?"* — and then, sharply: *"my big concern is that reflow2 operates exactly like it currently does now (how we are using it now). I don't do any authentication and I don't want to change that by adding in some authentication step."*

**RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.**

📌 Distinct from `req:the-hosted-surface-is-read-only-so-it-can-ship-before-authentication-exists`, which the guard offered and which was read before choosing: that requirement states what must be true of the first cut and treats authentication as ABSENT. This asks WHERE AUTHENTICATION SHOULD LIVE — a question that outlives the read-only cut, since delegated is not the same as missing.

═══ ⭐ FOR THE READ-ONLY SURFACE THE ANSWER IS YES, COMPLETELY ═══

The read-only surface needs one question answered: **who may REACH this server?** A network or proxy layer answers exactly that, and option (c)'s tailnet binding already does — a Tailscale/WireGuard peer is authenticated by the tunnel before a packet arrives.

**So the read-only surface needs ZERO authentication code in reflow2.** Not a workaround; the correct placement. It composes with what ships: `cap:remote-sessions`'s Host allowlist is DNS-rebinding protection, a different concern, still useful behind any proxy. The same holds for a reverse proxy doing OIDC on loopback. `rule:no-foreclosure` is satisfied — nothing about it prevents growing into a hosted multi-user service later.

═══ 🛑🛑 THE CORRECTION THAT MATTERS MOST: THE LINE IS REACHABILITY, NOT TRANSPORT ═══

**An earlier draft of this reasoning said "attributed writes over HTTP are refused unless reflow2 is told it is proxied". THAT WAS WRONG, and Anthony caught it by stating the constraint it violated.**

**His current daily setup IS HTTP.** `--shared` starts a detached server and proxies to it; every write in the 2026-08-26 session went through `http://127.0.0.1:40233/`. A rule keyed on "is this HTTP" would have broken the working local workflow — the precise outcome he was objecting to.

⭐ **THE DESIGN ALREADY DRAWS THE RIGHT LINE, AND NOBODY HAD NOTICED IT WAS THE SECURITY BOUNDARY.** The streamable-HTTP transport answers only requests whose Host header is on an allowlist — **`localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `::1` by default** — and reaching the server from another machine requires an explicit repeatable `--http-allow-host`. `cap:remote-sessions` (VERIFIED) says it in as many words: *"reaching the server from another machine is an explicit flag rather than a side effect of binding a public address."*

⇒ **So every write rule attaches to DELIBERATE REMOTE EXPOSURE, never to a transport:**

    stdio                                    → nothing changes
    --shared / loopback --http  (TODAY)      → nothing changes
    --http-allow-host <remote>               → the write rules apply

**He would never meet an authentication step, because he would never take the act that turns one on.** And if he did take it, he would have taken it deliberately — which is what makes the boundary honest rather than accidental.

📌 AND IT EXPLAINS WHY LOCAL NEEDS NO AUTHENTICATION AT ALL, EVER: a caller-supplied `contributor_id` is sound on a loopback surface precisely because anyone who can call that server can already edit the graph file directly. Authentication would add nothing but ceremony.

═══ THE LINE THAT REMAINS: MIDDLEWARE AUTHENTICATES A CONNECTION; IT CANNOT POPULATE A GRAPH FIELD ═══

    "MAY THIS CALLER REACH THE SERVER?"    → middleware's job, entirely. Tailnet, proxy, mTLS.
    "WHICH CONTRIBUTOR IS THIS, AND MAY    → NOT middleware's job. That identity must arrive
     THEY SETTLE INTENT?"                     INSIDE the tool call, as a `contributor_id` that
                                              `authored_by` and the confirmation ledger record.

A proxy can prove someone is Alex. **It cannot write `who:alex` into an `AUTHORED_BY` edge.** Today that argument is validated only for EXISTENCE (`require_contributor`), never for truth.

⇒ **Middleware removes the authentication problem and leaves the ATTRIBUTION problem exactly where it was.** They look like one problem and they are two.

═══ OPTIONS FOR THAT LAST HOP, none chosen, relevant only once REMOTE writes are wanted ═══

**(a) The proxy injects a trusted header** (`X-Forwarded-User`) mapped to a Contributor. Standard and cheap.
🛑 Trusting an injected header is sound *only behind a proxy*; bare on a port the same header is client-supplied and forgeable, against `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` (ENFORCED). If taken, it must be LOUD — reflow2 told explicitly, and REFUSING attributed writes when it has not been told. ⚠️ Residual risk reflow2 CANNOT check: a proxy that fails to strip a client-supplied header forges identity silently. That is a deployment property, and it should be stated in the design rather than discovered.

**(b) Mint-and-carry, as seats already do.** Consistent with `dec:stateless-seat-handle`; transport-independent. ⚠️ Counter: it moves the question to how the handle is OBTAINED, which is where the proxy returns.

**(c) The consuming app IS the Contributor.** Honest, and it collapses `loop_status(contributor_id=…)` and the confirmation ledger. `who:storyflow-api-boss` already carries this caveat; this makes it permanent.

⭐ **(d) THE REMOTE SURFACE MAY PROPOSE, NEVER SETTLE.** Remote writes land at `proposed`; approver edges and `accepted` status are refused, so settling intent still requires a session inside the machine boundary. **This needs NO new authorisation vocabulary** — `proposed` vs `accepted` already exists and the intent-authority gate already enforces it. It matches flo2's actual case (posting a brainstormed idea asserts nothing) and means the ENFORCED rule never depends on a network claim at all. ⚠️ Counter: Anthony could not approve anything from a web app, only propose. That is a real limit and his to weigh.

📌 **NOTHING HERE BLOCKS THE FIRST CUT.** The read-only surface ships without any of it.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SHARPENED 2026-09-22 — LEAVES ARE SERVERS, HUBS ARE THIN CLIENTS, AND A CLIENT MAY BE A CLIENT OF A CLIENT
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.

ANTHONY: "What if we treated the lowest levels of the graph as 'servers' and each hub/project-brain/management level as a 'thin-client'. This then turns the access question of the management level into a traditional server-client relationship and we can then use common API keys as the access/permission to the servers. The higher the levels then just get permissions to the management/sub-systems layers…kind of a client of a client?"

⭐ WHAT IT ADDS, AND IT IS A SIMPLIFICATION RATHER THAN A FEATURE: it turns the tier question from a GRAPH-TOPOLOGY problem into a CONNECTION problem. A hub that is a client needs no cross-graph edge, no mirrored copy and no new design vocabulary — it needs credentials. Taken together with his other lean the same day (the hub holds no design of its own, `dec:idea-a-graph-whose-children-are-themselves-reflow2-designs`), the two compose into one coherent picture: **the hub is a lens with credentials, and every node still lives in exactly one graph.**

📌 AND IT IS COMPATIBLE WITH HIS OWN CONSTRAINT AT THE TOP OF THIS NODE, which is worth stating because it reads like a reversal and is not. He said 2026-08-26: "I don't do any authentication and I don't want to change that by adding in some authentication step." The resolution is already above — **every write rule attaches to DELIBERATE REMOTE EXPOSURE, never to a transport.** stdio unchanged, `--shared`/loopback unchanged, `--http-allow-host <remote>` is where the rules engage. He would meet an API key only by taking the act that turns one on.

📌 MOST OF THE SHAPE IS ALREADY DECIDED, so this is a smaller proposal than it sounds:
  · `dec:central-host` (DECIDED, option c) — a hosted read/publish surface, one server per project on a tailnet.
  · `dec:one-process-many-stores` (ACCEPTED, conditional) — N single-writer stores in ONE process, one lock each, the directory stays the unit. ⚠️ NOTE THE WORD "SERVER" IS AMBIGUOUS BETWEEN THEM: his framing says each leaf graph IS a server; the accepted decision puts many stores behind one process. Both give a client one address per design to talk to, and they are not the same deployment. Worth being explicit about which before anyone builds.
  · `cap:select-graph-by-id` — a session names the design by `graph_id` and the server maps id to path. The client already says which server it wants.
  · `dec:the-registry-root-is-the-tenant-boundary` (DECIDED) — "the registry ROOT is the tenant boundary — listing stays unfiltered, and **reflow2 still authenticates nothing**." A key would map to a root; the boundary object already exists.

🛑🛑 THE NEW HAZARD, AND IT IS CREATED BY THE CHAINING RATHER THAN BY THE KEYS: **A KEY SAYS WHICH CLIENT, NEVER WHICH PERSON — AND EACH HOP ERASES MORE OF THE PERSON.** The two-question split above ("may this caller reach the server" vs "which contributor is this") holds at one hop. Under a client-of-a-client chain, the LEAF sees only the credential of the hub immediately above it. A division reaching A5 through a group hub presents the hub's key; A5 has no way to know which engineer acted, and a shared team key has none either at depth one.

⇒ So the deeper the chain, the further the acting person is from the only identity the leaf can see. And `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` is ENFORCED and gated in CI: a settled node MUST carry a name. **A credential chain structurally cannot supply one.** This does not break the proposal; it means the proposal must not be read as solving attribution, and the temptation to read it that way grows exactly as the chain gets longer — which is the option (a) trap above arriving by delegation instead of by a forged header.

⭐ AND THE EXISTING ANSWER COMPOSES WITH IT UNCHANGED, WHICH IS THE GOOD NEWS:
  · The KEY authorises the connection. Middleware's job, entirely, at every hop.
  · The `contributor_id` arrives INSIDE the tool call and names the person — mint-and-carry, per `dec:stateless-seat-handle`, transport-independent and therefore chain-independent. It survives any number of hops precisely because it never travels as a credential.
  · ⭐ **OPTION (d) ABOVE GETS STRONGER UNDER CHAINING, NOT WEAKER.** "The remote surface may PROPOSE, never SETTLE." A chain of clients may file intent freely at `proposed`; settling still requires a session inside the machine boundary. That needs no new authorisation vocabulary, it makes the ENFORCED rule independent of every network claim in the chain, and it pairs exactly with the hub-holds-no-design lean: the hub proposes into the child, the child's owner settles.

⚠️ THE COUNTER THAT HAS TO BE WEIGHED, and it is recorded elsewhere in this design rather than invented here: `dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency` states that reflow2 "HAS NO AUTHENTICATION and cannot acquire one without becoming a different product". That is not an argument against API keys — it is an argument about WHERE THEY LIVE. Keys in middleware leave reflow2 exactly as it is. Keys in reflow2's domain model make it an identity provider, which is a different product and one nobody has asked for.

NOT ANSWERED, and each is cheap to answer before building:
  · Does a hub's key grant it the child's FULL surface, or a scoped subset? An org chart implies scoping; nothing here models it.
  · What does the leaf RECORD about a chained caller — the immediate client, the whole chain, or nothing? "Nothing" is the honest default today and would make a chained write untraceable.
  · Is the client-of-a-client hop real, or does the division simply hold keys to every leaf it is over? The flat version is simpler, loses the delegation point, and is probably right first.

═══ 2026-09-28 — THE FIRST REAL SELF-HOSTED TEAM SERVER ARRIVED, AND IT NEEDS THIS ANSWERED (Alex, GitHub issue #616, art:github-issue-616-oauth-resource-server) ═══

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Alex's team (about 8 people, a 1,173-node design) hosts reflow2 in a container behind a reverse proxy, an OAuth proxy and an OIDC identity provider. In his words: "Right now a signature can't be checked. `contributor_id` is whatever the caller types, so on a shared graph any agent can sign as any contributor, and nothing in reflow2 can tell ... Our proxy can't give us this — it can only prove *someone authorized* is calling, which is why we're forwarding `X-Auth-Request-User` into a server that ignores it. That seems like the real motivation. Access control is the boring half."

MEASURED the same day (fact:root-cause-an-exposed-server-accepts-any-callers-signature-because-the-boundary-where-write-rules-attach-was-named-and-no-rule-was-chosen-2026-09-28): on a server exposed with --http-allow-host, an anonymous caller wrote a requirement as ACCEPTED signed by another contributor, and got no refusal and no note. His case is exactly the "last hop" above. It is no longer hypothetical.

A NEW OPTION, his, beside (a)–(d):
(e) REFLOW2 VERIFIES A SIGNED TOKEN ITSELF. An operator flag names an OIDC issuer and audience. reflow2 validates the Bearer JWT's signature, iss, aud and exp, derives the contributor from a verified claim through a configured mapping, and refuses or flags a contributor_id or approver that disagrees. This is a resource server, not an identity provider: no sign-in flow, no sessions, no user table. It is the only option that makes the signature checkable INSIDE reflow2, with no trusted header in the path.
Counter: token verification IS authentication in reflow2. That contradicts dec:the-registry-root-is-the-tenant-boundary (accepted: "REFLOW2 HAS NO AUTHENTICATION AND IS NOT GETTING ANY") and the architecture Anthony settled in flo2's graph on 2026-09-20 ("reflow2 stays an ENGINE and grows no authentication"). Taking (e) means reopening that ruling, which is Anthony's call.

WHAT HIS CASE DOES TO THE EXISTING OPTIONS:
· (a) the trusted header is now concrete, and cheap: his proxy ALREADY sends X-Auth-Request-User. A flag such as `--trust-identity-header <name>`, refused unless given and loud in the handshake, would give his team attribution AND authority with no authentication code in reflow2. The residual risk recorded above stands unchanged: a proxy that fails to strip a client-sent header forges identity, and reflow2 cannot check that.
· (d) propose-never-settle would stop the forgery outright on his server. The cost recorded above also stands: nobody could approve from the team server, only from inside the machine boundary, and for a team of 8 with no single machine that may be the wrong trade.
· The DISCOVERY half of his ask (a 401 that names where to sign in, and /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource) is what lets an MCP client run the OAuth flow itself instead of people pasting tokens. It can live in the gateway under the settled ruling. The accepted req:a-local-client-works-against-a-remote-reflow2-server-by-url, point 1, already asks reflow2's own --remote client to support "a sign-in flow (browser or device code) for a server that offers one", which would also end the token pasting for anyone who connects through reflow2's client.

SIZE, AS INFORMATION: (a) is small, a flag and one read site. (e) is medium: JWKS fetch and cache, validation, a claim-to-contributor mapping, and the metadata endpoint. Discovery alone is small. None of this is chosen.
properties.name: SETTLED 2026-09-28 — option (e) with a rule for every exposure: local stays unchanged; an exposed server verifies a Bearer token itself (an OAuth resource server, never an identity provider), or declares a trusted gateway, or refuses every settling write
properties.rationale:
Recorded because the question has a genuinely good answer for the case being shipped and a partial one for the case after it, and conflating those would be expensive in the way this project keeps finding.

The two-question split is the whole content: "may this caller reach the server" and "which contributor is this" look like one problem and decompose cleanly. Middleware owns the first completely; the second has to cross into the graph as a field, which no network layer can do on reflow2's behalf.

Option (a)'s trap is written at length rather than noted, because trusting an injected header is the obvious implementation and its failure mode is silent: the same binary is safe behind a proxy and forgeable without one, with nothing in the design saying which situation it is in. That is the shape `req:no-silent-fallback` exists for, and it lands on an ENFORCED rule.

The `dec:stateless-seat-handle` caveat is recorded as a re-read rather than a contradiction, because that decision's header objection was about client-supplied headers and a proxy-injected one is a different object — a distinction that is real, convenient, and therefore one somebody should make deliberately.
